t: The name Picti appears in Roman sources from the end of the third century AD as an outsiders' term for unromanised people in northern Britain, and was most likely pejorative.
From the seventh century the kingdom of Fortriu, centred on Moray, dominated Pictland, and in the ninth century the Pictish kingdom merged with Dál Riata to form the Kingdom of Alba.

The Pictish language, an Insular Celtic language related to Brittonic, was gradually displaced by Gaelic from the late ninth century, and Pictish identity was forgotten, probably during the 11th century.
dyk: The Latin word Picti is most commonly explained as meaning 'painted', yet the nobles, hunters and warriors carved on Pictish stones are shown without obvious tattoos.
ev: The Latin name Picti first appears in a Roman panegyric
A monastery is founded at Portmahomack, in an area once assumed to be among the last converted
Bridei mac Beli defeats the Northumbrians at the Battle of Dun Nechtain, halting their northward expansion
Nechtan mac Der Ilei is reported to have expelled the monks and clergy of Iona
Óengus mac Fergusa reigns as Pictish king and holds Dál Riata subject
Vikings kill the King of Fortriu, Eógan mac Óengusa, and the King of Dál Riata in a major battle
Kenneth MacAlpin becomes king of the Picts
Under Caustantín mac Áeda outsiders begin to call the region the Kingdom of Alba

f.homeland: Scotland north of the Firth of Forth and the Forth-Clyde isthmus, outside Dál Riata in the west; the core of Fortriu lay around Moray and Inverness; sites include Burghead Fort, Portmahomack, Abernethy, Rosemarkie and Dunkeld
f.period: the name Picti from the late third century AD (first in a panegyric of 297); several chiefdoms, then the Verturian hegemony of Fortriu from the seventh century, lasting about 160 years; merger with Dál Riata into the Kingdom of Alba in the ninth century; Pictish identity forgotten, probably by the 11th century
f.known: Pictish symbol stones and cross-slabs; the Pictish Beast and the mirror and comb, double-disc and Z-rod and crescent and V-rod symbols; heavy silver chains; penannular brooches and the St Ninian's Isle Treasure; the Battle of Dun Nechtain in 685; an Insular Celtic language now extinct
f.sources: outside writers: Roman panegyrics and Claudian, Bede's Ecclesiastical History, Adomnán's life of Columba, the Irish annals and the Pictish Chronicle; the stones and their inscriptions in Latin and ogham; excavations such as Martin Carver's at Portmahomack; a 2023 study of eight whole genomes from Lundin Links and Balintore
